title: Leave People With Their Dignity
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: The author argues that a technically accurate correction can still fail because it ignores the social cost of being corrected — once someone feels humiliated, they're managing their exposure in front of an audience, not just the original mistake, which produces defensiveness that looks like an inability to accept criticism but is often a predictable response to how the correction was delivered. Drawing on Epictetus's image of a guide who leads a lost traveler back to the road rather than mocking him for straying, and on Seneca's comparison of correction to medicine rather than punishment, the piece distinguishes correcting a specific behavior from attacking a person's whole identity, arguing only the former leaves room for someone to actually change. Its most practically useful claim is about long-run incentives: every time someone admits a mistake, they learn something about what happens next, and a pattern of humiliating people teaches them to become more secretive rather than more careful. The essay closes by reframing the issue as a test of the corrector's own character.
points: A correction that's factually right can still fail because it forces the other person to defend their sense of exposure or embarrassment, not just the original error.
Epictetus's image of a guide leading a lost traveler back to the road reframes correction as redirection, not a verdict to be delivered and walked away from.
Correcting a specific behavior leaves someone something to fix; attacking their character asks them to defend an identity instead.
People calibrate what they'll admit to you based on what happened last time — repeated humiliation teaches people to hide mistakes, not make fewer of them.
Withholding gratuitous humiliation from someone who's already lost the argument is a decision about your own character, not a favor you owe them.
quotes: The moment someone feels humiliated, the mistake is no longer the only thing they are dealing with. They are also dealing with the fact that they feel exposed, diminished, or embarrassed in front of someone whose opinion matters to them.
A guide, when he has found a man out of the road leads him into the right way: he does not ridicule or abuse him and then leave him. Epictetus, Discourses, 2.12

You interrupted me repeatedly in that meeting, and I need you not to do that again gives the other person something specific to confront. You are an arrogant person who has no respect for anyone asks them to defend an identity.
Seneca approaches correction from another direction in On Anger. He argues that anger is unnecessary for dealing with wrongdoing and compares correction to medicine.
If every mistake becomes an occasion for ridicule or prolonged shame, people may not become more careful about making mistakes. They may become more careful about letting you see them.
Epictetus warns that abusive words strengthen an abusive character just as repeated actions strengthen any other habit. We are always practicing something in the way we respond.
We are not only deciding what they deserve. We are deciding what kind of person we will practice being while we have the upper hand.
